comparison_to_previous.reason: The causal clinical roles of all 13 elements were clarified: ten were left in the ranked diagnostic series, secondary hemophagocytic syndrome was defined as a possible complication, humoral immunity disorder as a concomitant condition, thyroid nodule as an incidental finding. Clinical facts, external sources and their identities have not been changed.

coverage_projection.rationale: B1 moved to H1; B2 — in H4; B3 — in H5; B4 — in H2; B5 — in H3. All connecting branches are preserved and the varying depth of source coverage is fixed in G5.

Autoinflammatory, autoimmune, and solid tumor diagnostic alternatives were transferred without loss; secondary hemophagocytic syndrome is considered a possible complication with a separate source gap.

Vascular inflammatory and thromboembolic mechanisms are preserved in the diagnostic series. A possible humoral immune deficiency was brought out as a concomitant condition, and a thyroid nodule - as an incidental finding; there are no condition-specific sources for these branches.

Potentially reversible infectious causes and drug fever are retained in the diagnostic series. A possible humoral immune deficiency is indicated as a concomitant condition, and a thyroid nodule is indicated as a separate finding; detailed actions are reserved for the profile source route.

Critical oncohematological, endovascular, deep infectious, vascular and oncological diagnostic alternatives are preserved; secondary hemophagocytic syndrome is indicated as a dangerous possible complication.

A possible humoral immune deficiency was retained as a concomitant condition, a thyroid nodule as an incidental finding, and a solid tumor and drug fever as diagnostic alternatives. B13 transferred to W6 and G4 as a quality control of laboratory data.
B13 is not used to explain fever, sweating, or splenomegaly. It has been completely migrated to check dates, statuses, units and reference intervals.

critical_gaps.question: Is there a morphologically accessible focus and what is the complete distribution of lymph nodes and spleen involvement?
critical_gaps.rationale: Without a complete review of CT and diagnostic material, it is impossible to classify lymphoma, verify Castleman disease, or select a valid biopsy target.

critical_gaps.question: Do fever, night sweats, and weight change meet the strict definition of systemic symptoms in lymphoma guidelines?
critical_gaps.rationale: The source recorded a temperature of up to 38 °C and night sweats without characteristics of intensity; lymphoma guidelines use a temperature of more than 38 °C, profuse night sweats, or a loss of more than 10% of body weight.

critical_gaps.question: Is there a profile data set and validated source for the assessment of hemophagocytic syndrome in an adult?
critical_gaps.rationale: The selected histiocytic neoplasia guideline mentions hemophagocytic syndrome only as a condition to exclude in the presence of an unexplained change in the complete blood count. Complete criteria for adults, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen and serial blood formula are not available in the package.

critical_gaps.question: What are the exact dates, methods, and laboratory reference intervals for LDH, β₂-microglobulin, IgA, procalcitonin, and biochemistry as of 07/31/2026?
critical_gaps.rationale: Lymphoma prognostic indices comparing LDH and β₂-microglobulin with laboratory cutoffs. Current clinical facts do not contain these limits. Nine units of biochemistry were renewed by the registry.

critical_gaps.question: What condition-specific sources and patient data are needed to rule out the infectious, autoimmune, and autoinflammatory mimics directly named in the criteria for Castleman disease?
critical_gaps.rationale: E-CAND-6 specifically requires the exclusion of uncontrolled infections, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, adult-onset Still disease, and other named mimics before classifying idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease. The current package does not contain condition-specific diagnostic algorithms for these branches; vascular, endocrine, solid tumor, drug-related and thromboembolic branches do not project here.

blocked_actions: Establishing a definitive diagnosis of lymphoma, Castleman disease, hemophagocytic syndrome, or other systemic disease.
Initiation of antitumor, immunosuppressive or other etiological treatment based on this candidate.
Staging or subtyping of lymphoid neoplasia without diagnostic material and consistent morphological assessment.
Using LDH, β₂-microglobulin, IgA, procalcitonin, and nine biochemical measures for categorical assessment relative to laboratory range without source reference intervals.
decision_readiness.rationale: The status of the available work candidate is calibrated to the level of previous clinical prioritization. H1 ranks first because of the combination of persistent fever, night sweats, mild splenomegaly, and the most comprehensive source-supported verification route. This priority organizes further diagnostic assessment and remains preliminary. Final diagnosis, subtyping, staging, and treatment remain blocked until tissue, imaging, cellular, and profile-source data are available.

external_evidence.applicability: Fever, night sweats, and splenomegaly justify this diagnostic route. The page defines the test method and does not diagnose lymphoma in this patient.
external_evidence.proposition: Initial evaluation for suspected lymphoma includes history of systemic symptoms, physical examination, complete blood count with morphology, biochemistry, serology, and imaging; histopathological examination of the appropriate biopsy is usually essential for diagnosis.
external_evidence.title: JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies, 2023: II. lymphoma—overview

external_evidence.applicability: In the clinical facts, a temperature of up to 38 °C and night sweats without characteristics of intensity are indicated. Available data do not allow automatic classification of systemic symptoms.
external_evidence.proposition: The lymphoma classification of systemic symptoms uses unexplained fever over 38°C, profuse night sweats, and unexplained loss of over 10% of usual body weight over six months.

external_evidence.applicability: Clinical facts have numbers LDH and β₂-microglobulin without dates and source reference intervals. The current candidate does not apply these indexes and uses the page to fix the gap.

external_evidence.applicability: Splenomegaly makes the splenic B-cell direction relevant. The patient has no documented clonal population, lymphocytosis, flow cytometry, bone marrow morphology, or spleen.
external_evidence.proposition: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires proper immunophenotyping, complete blood count with formula, biochemistry, and imaging. The diagnosis can be reasonably assumed by peripheral blood clonal small lymphoid cells or bone marrow with a consistent phenotype; the morphology of the spleen has the highest classification certainty.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: B-Cell Lymphomas, Version 4.2026

external_evidence.applicability: No biopsy material, target lymph node, or PET/CT were recorded in the clinical records. The page supports morphological verification and careful interpretation of metabolic imaging.
external_evidence.proposition: The initial diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma usually requires excisional lymph node biopsy; core biopsy may be sufficient for diagnostic material, while fine-needle aspiration is mostly insufficient. PET/CT is used for initial staging, taking into account possible accumulation during infection and inflammation.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Hodgkin Lymphoma, Version 2.2026

external_evidence.applicability: Fever, night sweats, numerical dynamics of C-reactive protein and ESR and splenomegaly give partial overlap with small criteria. In the clinical facts, there is no multinodular lesion and histology, so Castleman disease has a lower current weight.
external_evidence.proposition: Consensus criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major criteria: characteristic histopathological changes in the lymph node and enlarged nodes in at least two stations. Additionally, small criteria and exclusion of infectious, autoimmune, and lymphoproliferative mimics are required.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Castleman Disease, Version 2.2026

external_evidence.applicability: Fever and splenomegaly support targeted evaluation for secondary hemophagocytic syndrome as a possible critical hyperinflammatory complication. external_evidence.proposition: In the histiocytic neoplasia route, an unexplained change in the complete blood count is a reason to consider the bone marrow study to evaluate for hemophagocytic syndrome, histiocytic or concomitant myeloid neoplasia. The page does not provide full criteria for adults.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Histiocytic Neoplasms, Version 1.2026

external_evidence.applicability: Splenomegaly without analysis of the cell population does not allow selecting one splenic entity. The classification supports an integrated diagnostic approach and prevents premature subtyping.
external_evidence.proposition: WHO-HAEM5 distinguishes several mature splenic B-cell neoplasms, including hairy cell leukemia, splenic marginal zone lymphoma, splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli, and splenic diffuse small B-cell red pulp lymphoma. The distinction is based on cytology, immunophenotype, molecular features, and tissue context.
external_evidence.title: The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Lymphoid Neoplasms

workup.label: Identify a biopsy-accessible lesion and tissue verification
workup.rationale: Lymphoma and Castleman disease require sufficient diagnostic material. Morphology and immunophenotype should differentiate between mature lymphoid neoplasm, reactive process, and the histologic spectrum of Castleman disease.

workup.label: Full review CT dated 04/16/2026
workup.rationale: Accurate dimensions of the spleen, all lymphatic stations, characteristics of the thyroid nodule, completeness of coverage, and contrast parameters are required. This will determine the presence of a biopsy target and verify the multicentric Castleman disease criterion.

workup.label: Hematological and immunoprotein characteristics of blood
workup.rationale: Complete blood count with formula and smear, flow cytometry as indicated, quantitative immunoglobulins, electrophoresis, and immunofixation may reveal a clonal population or a polyclonal immunoprotein pattern. These results distinguish between mature lymphoid neoplasm and Castleman disease within the exact positions of E-CAND-1, E-CAND-4, E-CAND-6, and E-CAND-8.

workup.label: Standardized description of systemic symptoms
workup.rationale: Maximum documented temperature, intensity of night sweats, change in body weight, and temporal relationship of symptoms are required. A temperature of up to 38 °C and a record of night sweats do not automatically allow strict lymphoma definition of systemic symptoms to be applied. This step refines the characteristic of H1 and is not used as an independent differentiator of H1 and H6.
workup.trigger: Perform if the evaluation of systemic symptoms affects the working H1 classification or the subsequent lymphoma classification after tissue verification.

workup.label: Review of criteria for Castleman disease
workup.rationale: For the multicentric form, confirm characteristic lymph-node histology and lymphadenopathy in at least two nodal stations, then evaluate minor criteria and exclusionary conditions, including human herpesvirus type 8-associated process, infection, autoimmune disease, and lymphoma.

workup.label: Source reconciliation of laboratory dates, units, and reference intervals
workup.rationale: Dates, methods and reference intervals for LDH, β₂-microglobulin, IgA, procalcitonin and biochemistry from 07/31/2026 need to be confirmed. The nine units deterministically recovered by the registry are used only for analysis identification and longitudinal grouping.

workup.label: PET/CT to locate the active lesion
workup.rationale: PET/CT can determine the distribution of active lesions and help select the biopsy site. Inflammatory or infectious accumulation is also possible, so each atypical site must be confirmed clinically or morphologically.
workup.trigger: Consider after full review of CT if fever persists, biopsy target is unclear, or clinical suspicion for systemic lymphoproliferative disease remains high.

workup.label: Evaluate the bone marrow
workup.rationale: Morphology, flow cytometry and trepanobiopsy can clarify bone marrow lesions and delineate splenic B-cell neoplasm. For hemophagocytic syndrome, this step is part of a broader assessment and does not replace specific criteria.
workup.trigger: Consider for clonal signal in peripheral blood, unexplained blood cell change, suspicious bone marrow findings on imaging, or need to classify splenic lymphoid neoplasia.

workup.label: Clinical assessment of infectious safety for H2 and H3
workup.rationale: Patient records record persistent fever, prior meropenem and vancomycin therapy, and absence of blood cultures, echocardiography, HIV status, TB route, and target microbiology results in the current package. E-CAND-6 only supports the mandatory exclusion of uncontrolled infections among Castleman disease mimics. A specific infection algorithm must be determined visually and supported by separate condition-specific sources.
workup.trigger: Immediate ocular evaluation is required for hemodynamic instability, new organ dysfunction, signs of sepsis, embolic manifestations, or new valvular signs; in a stable condition, urgent recovery of the infectious route through a responsible clinician is required.

reasoning_log.disclaimer: It is a coherent clinical reconstruction based on recorded data, source review decisions, and independent critique. It explains the differential diagnosis, the clinical roles of concomitant conditions, and the basis for the leading diagnostic hypothesis. The clinician determines the final diagnosis and treatment decision.

narrative.text: The clinical investigation concerns a 55-year-old patient with fever of unknown origin since April 2026, maximum recorded temperature up to 38 °C and night sweats. The duration of symptoms and their systemic nature require simultaneous evaluation of malignant, infectious, autoimmune, autoinflammatory, and vascular causes. The current temperature profile, intensity of sweating, change in body weight and new local symptoms remain unknown, so the clinical course needs to be updated.

The inflammatory activity varied widely, with C-reactive protein varying from 217.97 mg/L on 15 April to 673.1 mg/L on 23 May, 399 mg/L on 8 June, and 57.9 mg/L on 29 June. ESR was 62–66 mm/h in June. CT dated April 16 described mild splenomegaly and a nodular mass in the left lobe of the thyroid gland. This combination supports a systemic diagnostic workup, although no single finding determines the cause of the syndrome.

A broad differential search retained ten diagnostic categories. These include mature lymphoid neoplasm, endovascular and deep occult infections, systemic autoinflammatory syndrome, systemic autoimmune process, Castleman disease, systemic vasculitis, solid tumor with neoplastic fever, drug fever, and thromboembolic or other sterile vascular process. Their order reflects the combined clinical support and completeness of the available evaluation, leaving each direction open to new data.

The leading hypothesis is mature lymphoid neoplasm with splenic or bone marrow involvement. Fever, night sweats, and splenomegaly form a compatible lymphoproliferative pattern. Splenic marginal zone lymphoma and other mature B-cell neoplasms remain working options; Hodgkin lymphoma and aggressive B-cell lymphomas also require exclusion. LDH 410.8 U/L and β₂-microglobulin 2.28 mg/L are kept as incomplete supporting laboratory findings because dates and reference intervals are missing.

Lymphoma guidelines support a sequence of verification through history of systemic symptoms, examination, complete blood count with morphology, biochemistry, imaging, and adequate biopsy. For splenic B-cell neoplasms, cytology, immunophenotype, molecular features, and tissue context are decisive. In this case, there is no clonal cell population, flow cytometry, bone marrow morphology, or tissue. The sources justify the method of verification, and the clinical diagnosis remains preliminary.

The second- and third-ranked diagnoses are infective endocarditis or other endovascular infection and mycobacterial, fungal or other deep occult infection. Prior treatment with meropenem and vancomycin did not establish a conclusive cause for the fever. The results of blood cultures, their time relative to antibiotics, echocardiography, valvular risks, and peripheral vascular manifestations are not available. A negative PCR for cytomegalovirus evaluates a single pathogen at a specific time point and does not exclude tuberculosis, fungal disease, or another occult infection.

The fourth, fifth, and sixth positions cover adult-onset Still disease or other systemic autoinflammatory syndrome, systemic connective tissue disease or immune complex process, and Castleman disease. The magnitude of C-reactive protein variation supports an autoinflammatory pathway, but there is no ferritin, typical temperature pattern, rash, arthritis, or sore throat. Antinuclear antibodies of 1:320 support autoimmune testing, whereas specific antibodies, complement, urine profile, and organ manifestations are absent. For Castleman disease, characteristic lymph-node histology and lymphadenopathy in at least two nodal stations are not shown.

emphasis_terms: thromboembolic or other sterile vascular process
narrative.text: Lower positions retain clinically important mechanisms. A seventh is large-vessel vasculitis or other systemic vasculitis: age 55 years and ESR 62–66 mm/h support further evaluation, although vascular symptoms and targeted imaging are absent. The eighth is a solid tumor with neoplastic fever without a defined causative lesion. The ninth remains drug fever; known antibiotics were prescribed after the onset of symptoms, and the complete prior medication history is unknown. The tenth is a thromboembolic or other sterile vascular process with minimal direct support.

The three clinical entities are considered separately from the ranked diagnoses. Secondary hemophagocytic syndrome is a possible critical hyperinflammatory complication of an infection, malignancy, or autoimmune process; checking it does not eliminate the need to find the trigger. A possible humoral immune deficiency is a concomitant condition that can contribute to infectious or autoimmune manifestations. Nodular formation of the left lobe of the thyroid gland remains an incidental finding of uncertain nature without a proven causal relationship with systemic symptoms.

Source comparison most fully supports hematologic oncology pathway, Castleman disease criteria, and classification of splenic B-cell neoplasms. For endovascular and deep infections, adult-onset Still disease, systemic autoimmune diseases, vasculitis, tumor and drug fever, thyroid pathology and thromboembolic conditions, the source support remains incomplete. LDH, β₂-microglobulin, IgA, and procalcitonin cannot be categorically compared to laboratory limits without dates, methods, and reference intervals.

The first key step is a complete review of the protocol and images of CT dated April 16, 2026. Accurate dimensions of the spleen, description of all lymphatic stations, characteristics of the thyroid nodule, completeness of coverage, and contrast parameters are required. This review should identify a biopsy-accessible lesion and verify the multicentric Castleman disease criteria. If there is a suitable target, tissue verification with morphology and immunophenotyping is performed.

The second block of examination should cover complete blood count with differential, manual smear evaluation, reticulocytes, and flow cytometry as indicated. Quantitative IgA, IgG, and IgM, electrophoresis, and immunofixation will help assess a clonal or polyclonal immunoprotein pattern. Original laboratory forms must confirm dates, methods, units, and reference intervals. Bone marrow evaluation is considered for clonal signal, unexplained blood cell changes, or need to classify splenic lymphoid neoplasia.

The infectious direction requires multiple sets of blood cultures with precise timing relative to antibiotic exposure, echocardiography, and valvular risk assessment. Epidemiologic history should include tuberculosis contacts, travel, animal and occupational exposures, and immunosuppression; further microbiology is determined by localization features. Autoinflammatory and autoimmune areas require ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, liver function tests, antibodies to double-stranded DNA, a panel of antibodies to extracted nuclear antigens, C3, C4, and urinalysis.

A separate safety assessment addresses possible secondary hemophagocytic syndrome: ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, coagulogram, and serial complete blood count with formula are required along with a search for an infectious, malignant, or autoimmune trigger. The accompanying immune status is clarified by a repeated profile of immunoglobulins and a history of recurrent infections. Thyroid nodule requires TSH, free T4 and standardized ultrasound; fine-needle aspiration biopsy is determined by ultrasound features and size.

Independent clinical critique confirmed retention of the broad differential diagnosis, all causal relationships, nine diagnostic steps, and five key gaps. No premature shutdowns, unsupported connections, source drift, or loss of critical paths were detected. Causal roles were checked separately: secondary hemophagocytic syndrome remained a complication, a possible humoral immune deficiency was a concomitant condition, and a thyroid nodule was an incidental finding.

Critical revision also confirmed the continuous order of the ten diagnostic explanations and the retention of drug fever and sterile vascular process in the ranked order. The findings of the sources were not transferred to a specific patient without clinical comparison. The eight selected source propositions are associated with a corresponding check or gap. There are no unresolved critical or significant comments after the inspection; this result is not a medical acceptance of the diagnosis.

A mature lymphoid neoplasm with splenic or bone marrow involvement remains the leading working hypothesis because it best combines persistent fever, night sweats, splenomegaly, and the available route of verification. Current confidence allows for further investigation, but does not allow for definitive diagnosis, subtype, stage, or initiation of disease-specific treatment. Complete imaging evaluation, biopsy target determination, and consistent morphologic and cellular verification remain critical.

The working assessment should be reassessed after receiving a complete CT, morphology and immunophenotype, extensive blood work, microbiological and echocardiographic evaluation, profiled autoimmune and autoinflammatory parameters, accurate laboratory references and a current description of symptoms. The appearance of hemodynamic instability, new organ dysfunction, signs of sepsis, embolic or valvular manifestations requires urgent in-person clinical assessment. Re-prioritization should be based on a consistent comparison of new tissue, cellular, microbiological, imaging and laboratory findings with current symptoms. The material remains a working clinical reconstruction for the clinician review and is not a confirmed diagnosis or treatment.

The lymphoma classification of systemic symptoms uses unexplained fever over 38°C, profuse night sweats, and unexplained loss of over 10% of usual body weight over six months. Lymphoma prognostic indices use LDH and β₂-microglobulin relative to the upper limit of the laboratory interval along with histology, stage, and other clinical parameters.
source_library.title: JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies, 2023: II. lymphoma—overview

source_library.applicability: Splenomegaly makes the splenic B-cell direction relevant. The patient has no documented clonal population, lymphocytosis, flow cytometry, bone marrow morphology, or spleen.
source_library.proposition: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires proper immunophenotyping, complete blood count with formula, biochemistry, and imaging. The diagnosis can be reasonably assumed by peripheral blood clonal small lymphoid cells or bone marrow with a consistent phenotype; the morphology of the spleen has the highest classification certainty.
source_library.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: B-Cell Lymphomas, Version 4.2026

source_library.applicability: No biopsy material, target lymph node, or PET/CT were recorded in the clinical records. The page supports morphological verification and careful interpretation of metabolic imaging.
source_library.proposition: The initial diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma usually requires excisional lymph node biopsy; core biopsy may be sufficient for diagnostic material, while fine-needle aspiration is mostly insufficient. PET/CT is used for initial staging, taking into account possible accumulation during infection and inflammation.
source_library.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Hodgkin Lymphoma, Version 2.2026

source_library.applicability: Fever, night sweats, numerical dynamics of C-reactive protein and ESR and splenomegaly give partial overlap with small criteria. In the clinical facts, there is no multinodular lesion and histology, so Castleman disease has a lower current weight.
source_library.proposition: Consensus criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major criteria: characteristic histopathological changes in the lymph node and enlarged nodes in at least two stations. Additionally, small criteria and exclusion of infectious, autoimmune, and lymphoproliferative mimics are required.
source_library.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Castleman Disease, Version 2.2026

source_library.applicability: Fever and splenomegaly support targeted evaluation for secondary hemophagocytic syndrome as a possible critical hyperinflammatory complication. The available complete blood count has one time slice without a formula; the source supports only the conditional bone marrow step and captures the need for a separate profile source.
source_library.proposition: In the histiocytic neoplasia route, an unexplained change in the complete blood count is a reason to consider the bone marrow study to evaluate for hemophagocytic syndrome, histiocytic or concomitant myeloid neoplasia. The page does not provide full criteria for adults.
source_library.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Histiocytic Neoplasms, Version 1.2026

source_library.applicability: Splenomegaly without analysis of the cell population does not allow selecting one splenic entity. The classification supports an integrated diagnostic approach and prevents premature subtyping.
source_library.proposition: WHO-HAEM5 distinguishes several mature splenic B-cell neoplasms, including hairy cell leukemia, splenic marginal zone lymphoma, splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli, and splenic diffuse small B-cell red pulp lymphoma. The distinction is based on cytology, immunophenotype, molecular features, and tissue context.
source_library.title: The 5th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: Lymphoid Neoplasms
